A0022.title: Traffic Encryption
A0022.definition: Encrypting network request traffic or response traffic.
A0022.description: Traffic encryption typically provides a protection mechanism for process security. By encrypting data during transmission, attackers cannot directly obtain the original data or directly modify it.
A0022.limitation: Traffic encryption increases the complexity and cost of data transmission. When using traffic encryption, the trade-off between security and performance impact needs to be considered.

A0022-001.title: Transport Protocol Encryption
A0022-001.definition: Using standard TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 to protect data in transit, with mutual TLS or standard application-layer encryption where stronger peer authentication or sensitive-field protection is required.
A0022-001.description: Transport protocol encryption should use publicly reviewed TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3, correctly validate the server certificate, hostname, and certificate chain, and disable obsolete protocols, weak cipher suites, and insecure downgrade paths. Mutual TLS (mTLS) can validate client certificates when service-to-service interfaces require mutual authentication. Sensitive fields that must remain confidential across proxies, gateways, or intermediate processing stages can use a standard, mature application-layer encryption scheme in addition to TLS, backed by separate key generation, storage, rotation, and revocation controls. Custom cryptographic algorithms, proprietary handshakes, and modified SSL/TLS/HTTPS must not replace standard protocols because they lack adequate public review and can introduce hidden design and implementation flaws.
A0022-001.limitation: TLS primarily protects the confidentiality and integrity of data while it traverses the network. If an endpoint, server, or trusted proxy is compromised, plaintext may still be stolen before encryption or after decryption. Certificate-validation errors, protocol downgrade, weak cipher suites, and poor key management can weaken or nullify the protection. Encrypted traffic also exposes metadata such as endpoints, timing, and volume that can support traffic analysis. mTLS and application-layer encryption add certificate and key lifecycle overhead, and application-layer encryption does not replace correctly configured TLS.

A0022-002.title: Request Data Encryption
A0022-002.definition: Encrypting request data sent to the server to prevent interception or tampering during transmission.
A0022-002.description: Request data encryption refers to encrypting the request body on top of an existing protocol (such as HTTPS) before sending it to the server, to ensure data is not stolen or tampered with during transmission. It is commonly used on coupon-claiming, ordering, payment, and authentication APIs to prevent attackers from reading parameters through packet capture, changing amounts, tampering with redemption codes, and replaying requests. It can be applied in any business scenario, but requires server-side decryption logic and should be combined with API signatures, replay protection, and server-side business validation.
A0022-002.limitation: Generally implemented by hooking the remote request function to encrypt data, but this may cause certain compatibility issues. If some business logic does not use a unified remote request function, that portion of data cannot be encrypted. Client-side encryption algorithms and key-derivation logic can still be recovered through decompilation, dynamic debugging, or Frida hooks; after plaintext parameters are recovered, attackers may still forge encrypted requests, so this cannot replace server-side permission, amount, and inventory checks.

A0022-003.title: Response Data Encryption
A0022-003.definition: Encrypting response data from the server to prevent interception or tampering during transmission.
A0022-003.description: Response data encryption refers to encrypting the response body on the server side to ensure data is not stolen or tampered with during transmission. It is commonly used to protect activity inventory, prices, risk-control decisions, entitlement status, and other returned content, reducing the efficiency of packet-capture analysis, client-side display tampering, and automation-script development. It can be applied in any business scenario, but requires client-side decryption logic and should be paired with code obfuscation, key protection, and integrity checks.
A0022-003.limitation: Generally implemented by hooking the remote request function to encrypt data, but this may cause certain compatibility issues. If some business logic does not use a unified remote request function, that portion of data cannot be encrypted. Because response decryption logic must run on the client, attackers can recover plaintext and keys through decompilation, dynamic debugging, or hooking the decryption function; once reversed, response encryption raises analysis cost but cannot stop direct server-side API calls.

A0022-004.title: Custom Transport Protocol
A0022-004.definition: A non-standard communication protocol, self-developed or derived from modifying a standard protocol at the transport or application layer, that prevents conventional packet-capture and protocol-parsing tools from directly recovering business data.
A0022-004.description:
A custom transport protocol privatizes protocol headers, handshake flows, field layouts, or encryption algorithms (such as modified TLS handshakes, custom binary frames, or proprietary message encapsulation) so that client-server traffic no longer follows public specs like HTTP/TLS. Even if an attacker captures the traffic with Wireshark or Charles, they see only meaningless binary or encrypted payloads and must reverse-engineer the client's parsing logic before recovering request parameters and response contents.

It is commonly paired with transport protocol encryption (A0022-001) and request data encryption (A0022-002) to cover apps, mini-programs, and client SDKs in non-browser scenarios, materially raising the cost for illicit actors to write automation scripts or launch protocol-level attacks. Because the client must embed the parsing code, the security ultimately depends on whether that logic can be effectively obfuscated and protected against hooking.
A0022-004.limitation: The client-embedded parsing logic can be recovered by attackers via reverse compilation, hooking remote request functions, or dynamic injection tools like Frida; once the algorithm or key is extracted, legitimate packets can be forged at scale and all custom-protocol protection collapses. It is also inapplicable to browser web access, and inconsistent client-server protocol versions cause communication failures, raising maintenance and gray-release cost.
